newsitem.title: KENYA: Students clash with Kenya police, burn vehicles.
newsitem.headline: Students clash with Kenya police, burn vehicles.

text.p: Students on a second campus of Nairobi University clashed with police on Wednesday and set vehicles ablaze as violence spread over calls for constitutional reforms, witnesses said.

The clashes at Kabete campus 16 km (10 miles) northwest of Nairobi took place as a heavily armed paramilitary force stormed the main campus in the city centre, breaking down doors, looting and vandalising student rooms, the witnesses said.

Scores of students, including one who was clubbed heavily as reporters watched, were wounded in the mayhem at the main campus. The violence forced the government of President Daniel arap Moi to close the university.
Nine people were killed in Kenya on Monday during the most violent clashes between police and protesters since unrest in 1991 that helped push Moi to allow multi-party elections.
A Nairobi resident told Reuters by telephone that students at Kabete fought running battles with police and set a bus and government car on fire before police retreated.
Police spokesman Assistant Commissioner Peter Kimanthi declined to comment on the police brutality at the university.
A 20-year-old civil engineering student, Cyril Kiplimo, described the situation as "completely chaotic".
"The police are beating people, anyone in sight, they are firing teargas," he said.

A Reuters correspondent saw police beat students. A third-year student identified as F.W. Kinyanjui by his colleagues was beaten repeatedly on the back of his head and taken away unconscious in an ambulance.
Reporters also saw police break down doors in the halls of residence. Students were dragged out and clubbed while their possessions were vandalised and some taken away by police.
Earlier, Kenyan authorities closed the university after students marched into the city centre following a call for more protests by opposition groups demanding constitutional reforms.

A statement by the university Vice-Chancellor, Francis Gichaga, said the closure was made necessary by the deteriorating situation on the main campus as political tension rose in the East African country.

"Despite the appeal for calm in the circular of 8th July and the address by the vice-chancellor, the situation has continued to deteriorate...the University of Nairobi will be closed with immediate effect," Gichaga said in a statement.
The university has 19,000 students. Its closure had been widely expected since last weekend when political unrest broke out in Kenya.
Heavily armed police and other units patrolled the streets of Nairobi and more reinforcements were being moved into the city centre.
Earlier on Wednesday, students took to the streets to protest reports that four colleagues had died of wounds in clashes with police during protests on Monday.
But police spokesman Kimanthi denied the report in the independent Daily Nation newspaper, describing it as "pure falsehood".
Kimanthi told Reuters in a telephone interview that only two students died in incidents completely unrelated to the protests on Monday.

He said one student died at the city's Kenyatta National Hospital in circumstances still unknown, while another was knocked down by a hit-and-run truck. Kimanthi said police were looking into both incidents.

Opposition parties, human rights groups and other bodies under the umbrella National Convention Executive Committee (NCE) had called for protests on Wednesday to press the government for constitutional reforms before elections.

Reformists want the repeal of six laws from colonial times including the Public Order Act used to regulate public gatherings. They are also demanding free access to state-controlled media, particularly radio, and changes in the electoral law.
No date has been set for the parliamentary and presidential polls in which Moi, 73, is still widely expected to win another five-year term because of squabbling among opposition leaders.
